findings.change: Add worked mechanism on Type 1 vs Type 2 CPU trap handling and hardware virtualization execution
findings.anchor_str: The Linux KVM Subsystem and QEMU Userspace Model
findings.roadmap_study_clause: Hypervisors (Type 1 vs Type 2), what a VM actually is
findings.full_drafted_text:
Hypervisor execution models: hardware interception vs trap-and-emulate

  • What it is in general: Type 1 bare-metal hypervisors (KVM, ESXi) execute directly above hardware, utilizing hardware extensions (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) to transition CPU execution between VMX Root (hypervisor) and VMX Non-Root (guest) modes. Type 2 hypervisors execute atop a host OS, routing guest instructions through host syscalls. Sensitive CPU instructions trigger a VM-Exit hardware trap.
  • Relevance to a cloud architect: Understand the performance cost of VM-Exits. Workloads with high interrupt frequency or nested virtualization incur measurable virtualization overhead; paravirtualized virtio drivers minimize exits by using shared-memory ring buffers.
  • Relevance to GCP: Compute Engine instances run on Google's hardened KVM-based hypervisor. Nested virtualization allows running KVM inside Compute Engine VMs on supported machine types.
  • Concrete example: Inspect hypervisor capabilities from a Linux terminal: grep -E "(vmx|svm)" /proc/cpuinfo and check KVM node presence via ls -l /dev/kvm.
  • Evidence limit: Hardware flags verify CPU instruction support, not hypervisor scheduling policy or memory overcommit ratios.
  • Further study: KVM API description (accessed 2026-10-04)

findings.rule: TOPICS=expand; roadmap Study: Linux kernel namespaces: PID, net, mnt, IPC, UTS, user
findings.change: Add worked mechanism on kernel namespace inspection, clone flags, and user namespace UID/GID mappings
findings.roadmap_study_clause: Linux kernel namespaces: PID, net, mnt, IPC, UTS, user
findings.full_drafted_text:
Kernel namespace mechanics: isolation without virtualization

  • What it is in general: Linux namespaces partition global system resources into isolated abstractions. The seven core namespaces (PID, net, mnt, ipc, uts, user, cgroup) wrap global kernel resources so processes inside a namespace perceive private instances. The clone() and unshare() syscalls establish these boundaries.
  • Relevance to a cloud architect: Containers share the host kernel. Namespaces restrict visibility, not execution privilege. Root (UID 0) inside a container without user namespaces is host UID 0; a kernel exploit in any namespace compromises the host kernel.
  • Relevance to GCP: GKE nodes isolate pods using namespaces and cgroups. For multi-tenant clusters requiring true boundary isolation, GKE Sandbox (gVisor) intercepts syscalls via a userspace Sentry kernel.
  • Concrete example: Inspect active namespaces: lsns -t pid,net,mnt and compare process views via readlink /proc/50997/ns/*.
  • Evidence limit: Namespace inode uniqueness confirms separation of visibility, but does not enforce CPU, memory, or I/O resource limits.
  • Further study: namespaces(7) description (accessed 2026-10-04)

findings.roadmap_study_clause: cgroups v2 resource limits for CPU/memory; seccomp profiles and capabilities
findings.full_drafted_text:
cgroups v2 and seccomp: resource throttling and syscall filtering

  • What it is in general: cgroups v2 provides a unified hierarchy to meter and throttle memory (memory.max, memory.high), CPU (cpu.max, cpu.weight), and I/O. Seccomp (Secure Computing Mode) uses Berkeley Packet Filters (BPF) to intercept syscalls at the kernel entry point, returning EPERM or sending SIGSYS before execution.
  • Relevance to a cloud architect: Distinguish denial from starvation: cgroup limits cause CPU throttling or SIGKILL 137 (OOM), whereas seccomp blocks unauthorized syscalls (e.g. keyctl, ptrace) without killing the process unless configured.
  • Relevance to GCP: Cloud Run and GKE enforce default container seccomp profiles and drop dangerous Linux capabilities (e.g., CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_ADMIN) to protect node pools.
  • Concrete example: Check cgroup hierarchy version: stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup (cgroup2fs indicates v2). Verify dropped capabilities: capsh --print.
  • Evidence limit: cgroup counters verify current consumption against limits; seccomp audit logs require configured auditd/journalctl filters.
  • Further study: cgroups(7) description (accessed 2026-10-04)
